name: backtesting_validation.json
description: The full validation pipeline: exact rules, costs, out-of-sample discipline, overfitting traps and go-live checklists, with sourced walk-forward and data-snooping research context.
principle: A strategy is only believable after it survives realistic costs, out-of-sample data, randomness checks and a forward test. Most apparent edges disappear under these tests.

pipeline.name: Write exact rules
pipeline.detail: Entry, stop, target, sizing, filters, timeframe, instrument, session. No discretion. If a rule cannot be coded, it cannot be tested.

pipeline.name: State a hypothesis
pipeline.detail: Why should this work? Tie to a structural feature (regime persistence, spike frequency, risk premium). No reason = likely noise.

pipeline.name: Get clean data
pipeline.detail: Tick or candle history with correct timestamps; check gaps, duplicates, timezone. Use enough data: ideally 300+ trades and multiple regimes.

pipeline.name: Split data
pipeline.detail: In-sample (design, e.g. 60%), validation (20%), untouched out-of-sample (20%). Touch the out-of-sample set once.

pipeline.name: Backtest with costs
pipeline.detail: Include spread, slippage (add 0.5-1x spread extra), swap, commission. Use next-bar-open fills for signals computed on close.

pipeline.name: Baseline comparison
pipeline.detail: Compare to random entries with same exits and to buy-and-hold. If random entries perform similarly, the entry has no edge.

pipeline.name: Robustness tests
pipeline.detail: Parameter sensitivity, noise, cost stress, different instruments/time periods.

pipeline.name: Walk-forward analysis
pipeline.detail: Optimise on a window, test on the next window, roll forward; stitch out-of-sample results.

pipeline.name: Monte Carlo
pipeline.detail: Shuffle/resample trades to estimate drawdown and ruin distribution.

pipeline.name: Forward test on demo
pipeline.detail: 50-100+ trades with frozen rules; compare stats with backtest.

pipeline.name: Small live
pipeline.detail: 0.25% risk or less for 100 trades; scale only if live stats match tested expectations.

pipeline.name: Monitor and retire
pipeline.detail: Track rolling expectancy; stop or re-validate if performance degrades beyond tested drawdown.

metrics.name: Number of trades
metrics.note: Aim for 100 minimum, 300+ preferred; fewer trades give wide uncertainty.

metrics.name: Average win, average loss, payoff ratio
Profit factor
metrics.reading: Under 1 losing; 1.0-1.3 marginal after costs; 1.3-2.0 decent; very high values on few trades are suspicious.

metrics.name: Max drawdown
metrics.reading: Expect live drawdown to exceed backtest max by roughly 1.5-2x.

metrics.name: Average and max losing streak
metrics.note: Plan sizing for the Monte Carlo 95th percentile streak.

metrics.name: Sharpe ratio
metrics.reading: Above 1 good, above 2 excellent but verify; compute on equity-curve returns.

metrics.name: SQN (System Quality Number)
metrics.reading: Under 1.6 poor; 1.6-2.5 average; 2.5-3 good; above 3 excellent (Van Tharp heuristic).

metrics.name: t-statistic of mean R
metrics.reading: Above about 2 suggests the mean is unlikely zero by chance, but multiple-testing inflates this.

metrics.name: Confidence interval of win rate
metrics.example: 55% win rate over 100 trades has CI roughly 45%-65%, so 'edge' is unproven.

methods.name: In-sample / out-of-sample split
methods.how: Design on first segment; test on later, unseen segment. Keep time order; never shuffle time series for validation.
methods.pass_criteria: Out-of-sample expectancy positive and at least about 50% of in-sample; drawdown within 1.5x.

methods.name: Walk-forward optimisation
methods.how: Example: optimise on 6 months, trade the next 1 month, roll forward monthly. Collect out-of-sample months.
methods.metric: Walk-forward efficiency = out-of-sample annualised return / in-sample annualised return; above about 0.5 is encouraging.

methods.name: Purged / combinatorial cross-validation
methods.how: For ML-based signals: split into folds with embargo gaps so overlapping labels do not leak; evaluate across many train/test combinations.

methods.name: Monte Carlo trade resampling
methods.how: Randomly resample or reorder the list of trade R results 5,000-10,000 times; record final return, max drawdown, longest losing streak.
methods.use: Pick risk-per-trade so the 95th percentile drawdown stays below tolerance (e.g. 20%).

methods.name: Random trade skipping
methods.how: Randomly remove 10-20% of trades to see if profit depends on a few lucky trades.

methods.name: Parameter sensitivity / plateau test
methods.how: Vary each parameter +/-20-30%. A real edge shows a broad profitable plateau; a single spike of profit is overfitting.

methods.name: Cost stress test
methods.how: Double spread and slippage. If profits vanish, edge is too thin for live trading.

methods.name: Random entry baseline
methods.how: Use same stop/target/sizing but enter at random times matching your trade frequency; repeat 1,000 times. Your result should sit in the top 5% of the random distribution (permutation test).

methods.name: Return permutation / bootstrap
methods.how: Shuffle the signal relative to returns (or bootstrap returns) to build a null distribution for Sharpe or expectancy; compute p-value.

methods.name: Multiple-testing correction
methods.how: If you tried K strategies/parameter sets, the best result is biased upward. Use Bonferroni, White's Reality Check, or Deflated Sharpe Ratio (Bailey and Lopez de Prado) to adjust.
methods.rule: Keep a log of every variant tested.

methods.name: Regime split testing
methods.how: Evaluate results separately in trending, ranging, high-vol and low-vol periods; know where the strategy loses.

methods.name: Cross-instrument / cross-index test
methods.how: Test the same rules on related indices (e.g. V50, V75, V100). Robust ideas transfer with minor changes; for independent synthetic generators, results should differ only by volatility scaling.

methods.name: Forward/demo test
methods.how: Run frozen rules in real time. Compare slippage, fills, expectancy to backtest. Minimum 50-100 trades.

methods.name: Staged scaling
methods.how: Demo -> 0.25% risk -> 0.5% -> 1% only after each stage matches expectations over 100 trades.

overfitting_traps.fix: Use only data available at decision time; use previous bar values for signals; execute on next bar open.
Log every test; correct for multiple testing.
Verify indicators do not change past values.
Test across multiple periods and regimes.
Optimise for robust metrics like median expectancy under Monte Carlo.
When both stop and target are inside one candle, assume the worst (stop first) or use tick data.
Add slippage and spread; use ask for buys, bid for sells.

synthetic_index_specific: Because synthetic series are generated by a known stochastic process, you can generate your own simulated data with the same parameters and test whether a strategy has any edge; if it makes money on pure simulation it must be exploiting a designed feature, and if it fails there it cannot work on the real index.
Run the random-entry baseline on synthetic data first; for pure random walks nothing but costs matter and expectancy will be negative.
Check autocorrelation, Hurst, variance ratio before building indicator systems.
For regime-switching or spike products, validate the structural feature (drift per regime, spike probability) with large tick samples.
Use the exact broker spread/swap schedule; Deriv may change settings, so re-check periodically.
go_live_checklist: At least 100 backtest trades (300+ preferred) with costs.
Stable under parameter and cost stress.
Monte Carlo 95th percentile drawdown within personal limit.
50-100 forward demo trades consistent with backtest.
Risk plan: per-trade, daily, weekly, drawdown limits.

ai_model_rules: When asked 'does this strategy work?', answer that it must be tested and list the steps; do not claim it works.
When asked for win-rate claims, give ranges and uncertainty, not single guarantees.
If a user reports a great backtest, ask about costs, number of trades, out-of-sample, parameter count and multiple-testing.

research_context: Rigorous walk-forward frameworks are designed to mitigate overfitting and look-ahead bias; a single chronological holdout is a weaker but simpler alternative.
Repeated testing until something looks profitable is data snooping; probability-of-backtest-overfitting (PBO) style corrections exist for searches with known ground truth.
Overlapping labels (e.g. a 5-bar horizon on every bar) reduce the effective independent sample size below the nominal count.
application_to_this_app: ml_research.json uses overlapping 5-bar labels and reports this limit in its caveats; its screening gate is directional, not a profitability or significance test.
